meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I cannot tell a lie, I did it with my little hatchet'?
meta.ogDescription: George Washington never said it. Parson Weems invented the cherry-tree tale in 1806; the tidy popular line is a later paraphrase of his fiction.

answer.label: Not George Washington — invented by his biographer, Parson Weems
answer.authorDates: 1759–1825 · itinerant preacher, bookseller, and early Washington biographer
answer.sourceLine: Young George never said this. The whole cherry-tree confession was invented by Mason Locke ‘Parson’ Weems and first printed in the 5th edition of his Life of Washington in 1806 — eight years after Washington’s death. Weems’s own line reads “I can’t tell a lie, Pa; you know I can’t tell a lie; I did cut it with my hatchet”; the tidy popular form “I cannot tell a lie, I did it with my little hatchet” is a later, smoothed-down paraphrase spread by 19th-century schoolbooks. There is no historical evidence the episode ever happened.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: Invented moral anecdote — no historical basis

source.excerpt: “George,” said his father, “do you know who killed that beautiful little cherry tree yonder in the garden?” … looking at his father, with the sweet face of youth brightened with the inexpressible charm of all-conquering truth, he bravely cried out, “I can’t tell a lie, Pa; you know I can’t tell a lie. I did cut it with my hatchet.”
trail: The U.S. National Park Service states the tale was first published by Parson Weems in the 5th edition of his biography (1806) and that there is no historical evidence it happened — Weems’s only source was an anonymous, unnamed woman.
Wikipedia’s entry on Mason Locke Weems attributes the famous “I can’t tell a lie … I did cut it with my hatchet” confession to Weems’s Life of Washington.
A close reading at Plodding Through the Presidents confirms the story “was first put into print by Mason Locke Weems” in 1806 and that later retellings reshaped his original wording.
source.excerptNote: Weems’s own wording (5th ed., 1806). The familiar compressed form — “I cannot tell a lie, I did it with my little hatchet” — drops the address to “Pa,” smooths “did cut it” into “did it,” and adds “little” (Weems wrote just “my hatchet”).

source.rightsNote: The wording descends from Parson Weems’s The Life of Washington (5th edition, 1806) and its many 19th-century schoolbook retellings (notably McGuffey’s Readers from 1836) — all published well before 1931 and long in the public domain. The tidy popular short form is an anonymous later compression of Weems’s invented line, likewise of 19th-century vintage.

author.name: Mason Locke Weems
author.kicker: The true author of the words
author.heading: The man who invented the cherry tree
author.metaLine: 1759–1825 · American clergyman, book agent, and Washington biographer
author.bio: Mason Locke Weems (1759–1825), universally known as “Parson Weems,” was an Episcopal-ordained preacher turned traveling bookseller who wrote wildly popular, moralizing biographies. His Life of Washington first appeared in 1800 and went through dozens of editions; in the fifth edition of 1806 he added the cherry-tree anecdote to dramatize Washington’s honesty. Weems freely embellished for effect, and the story — sourced only to an unnamed elderly woman — is regarded by historians as his own invention rather than fact.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone credits Washington
misattribution.intro: The quote is doubly misattributed: it is pinned on a man who never said it, in a wording its own inventor never quite wrote.

items.why: Washington left no record of any cherry-tree confession, and both Mount Vernon and Ferry Farm treat it as legend. The National Park Service notes there is no historical evidence for it and that Weems’s source was an anonymous, unreliable witness.

Even setting aside that it is fiction, “I cannot tell a lie, I did it with my little hatchet” is not Weems’s sentence. Weems wrote “I can’t tell a lie, Pa; you know I can’t tell a lie; I did cut it with my hatchet”; the smoothed short form was spread by later schoolbooks such as McGuffey’s Readers and other retellings.

misattribution.truthLine: The words belong to a preacher-turned-bookseller writing moral fiction in 1806, not to the six-year-old Washington — and the version people quote is a paraphrase of even Weems’s own invented line.

context.heading: Why a made-up line stuck
lead: After Washington’s death in 1799, an eager public wanted intimate stories about the first president. Weems, a Federalist admirer of order and self-discipline, supplied them — casting Washington’s public greatness as the fruit of private virtue. The cherry tree, added in 1806, was the perfect parable of honesty.

Nineteenth-century schoolbooks, above all McGuffey’s Readers (from 1836), drilled the story into millions of American children and standardized its wording, which is how a bookseller’s moral fiction hardened into “something Washington said.”
context.pull: A bookseller’s parable, repeated until it passed for history.
